options: solves a Newton system with the Hessian
requires the feasible set to be a Euclidean ball
minimizes the linear model \(\nabla f(x)^T s\) over the set, then moves from \(x\) toward that \(s\)
projects \(x - \nabla f(x)\) onto the set
questions.explanation: The linear minimization oracle replaces the projection. The next point is a convex combination of \(x\) and the oracle's answer, so it stays in the set when the set is convex. Projecting a gradient step is the projected-gradient method. A Newton system uses a quadratic model. The oracle is useful on a simplex or an \(\ell_1\) ball, not only on a Euclidean ball.

questions.prompt: On the simplex \(x + y = 1\), \(x \ge 0\), \(y \ge 0\), start at \((1/2,\ 1/2)\) where the gradient is \((-1,\ 3)\). With step fraction \(1/2\), what is the first coordinate of the next point?
questions.explanation: The smaller gradient component is \(-1\), in the first coordinate, so the oracle returns \((1,\ 0)\). The update is \(\tfrac12 (1/2,\ 1/2) + \tfrac12 (1,\ 0) = (3/4,\ 1/4)\). The first coordinate is \(3/4\). Reporting \(1/4\) is the second coordinate. Reporting \(1\) is the oracle's first coordinate, which would be the full step \(\gamma = 1\). Reporting \(-1\) is the gradient component. The oracle minimizes the linear model, so it selects the smaller component.

questions.prompt: On the probability simplex, the linear minimization oracle returns
options: the Euclidean projection of the gradient onto the simplex
a standard-basis vector at a smallest gradient component
a standard-basis vector at a largest gradient component
the barycenter, for every gradient
questions.explanation: A linear function on a polytope attains its minimum at a vertex. On the simplex the vertices are the standard-basis vectors, and the linear value at \(e_i\) is the \(i\)-th gradient component. The minimum is the smallest component. The largest component maximizes the linear model. The barycenter ignores the gradient. A Euclidean projection is a different subproblem.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order of one conditional-gradient iteration. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The linear function is built from the gradient, so the gradient comes first. The direction points at the oracle's answer, so the oracle comes before the direction. The move uses the direction. An open-loop fraction such as \(2/(k+2)\) still multiplies a direction that has to be formed first. Projecting a gradient step is not one of these steps.

steps: Evaluate the gradient at the current feasible point.
Minimize the linear function defined by that gradient over the feasible set, and call the minimizer \(s\).
Form the direction from the current point to \(s\).
Move from the current point by a fraction of that direction, with the fraction in \((0,\ 1]\).

questions.prompt: On the probability simplex in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), the gradient is \((2,\ 2,\ 5)\). Which points minimize the linear model?
questions.explanation:
The linear value of a point is the gradient's product with that point.
• \((1,\ 0,\ 0)\) and \((0,\ 1,\ 0)\) each give \(2\).
• \((0,\ 0,\ 1)\) gives \(5\).
• \((1/2,\ 1/2,\ 0)\) gives \(2\).
• \((1/2,\ 0,\ 1/2)\) gives \(1 + 5/2 = 7/2\).
The minimum value is \(2\). Any convex combination of the minimizing vertices is also a minimizer. The oracle may return any of them.

questions.prompt: A conditional-gradient update with fraction \(g\) moves a coordinate from \(a\) toward the oracle value \(b\). The new coordinate equals
questions.explanation: The update is the convex combination \((1 - g) a + g b\). Every name appears. Using \(g a + (1 - g) b\) swaps the current point with the oracle point. Using \(a + b\) drops the fraction. Using \(g (b - a)\) is the displacement, not the new coordinate.

questions.prompt: A note runs the linear oracle on the probability simplex with gradient \((4,\ -1)\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The simplex and the gradient are as stated. Minimizing the linear model selects the smaller component, which is \(-1\), so the oracle returns \((0,\ 1)\). The vertex \((1,\ 0)\) maximizes the linear model. With fraction \(1\) the next point is whatever the oracle returned, so the fourth step is the right rule applied to the wrong vertex. The false claim is the choice of vertex.

steps: The feasible set is the probability simplex in \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
The linear oracle returns \((1,\ 0)\), because \(4\) is the larger component.
With fraction \(1\), the next point is the oracle's answer.
reasons: The oracle minimizes the linear model, so it returns \((0,\ 1)\), the vertex of the smaller component.
The gradient components are not \(4\) and \(-1\).
A fraction of \(1\) does not move all the way to the oracle's answer.

questions.prompt: The open-loop conditional-gradient fraction is \(2/(k + 2)\), with \(k\) counting from \(0\). What is that fraction at \(k = 6\)?
questions.explanation: The denominator is \(6 + 2 = 8\), so the fraction is \(2/8 = 1/4\). At \(k = 0\) the same formula equals \(1\), a full step to the oracle's answer. Reporting \(2/6\) uses \(k\) without the shift. Reporting \(1\) is the first fraction, not the fraction at step \(6\). Reporting \(8\) is the denominator. This number is a step fraction. It is not the function gap.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that drops at first and then flattens.

questions.prompt: On the \(\ell_1\) ball, the linear minimization oracle returns
options: \(\pm e_i\) at a coordinate of largest gradient magnitude, with the sign opposite the gradient
the Euclidean projection of \(-\nabla f\) onto the unit disk
the origin, for every nonzero gradient
a vector with every coordinate equal to the same nonzero value
questions.explanation: The \(\ell_1\) ball's extreme points are the signed standard-basis vectors. The linear value at \(\sigma e_i\) is \(\sigma g_i\), so the minimum uses the most negative product: the largest \(|g_i|\), with \(\sigma = -\mathrm{sign}(g_i)\). A Euclidean projection is the oracle for a disk. The origin has linear value zero, which is worse than a negative value. Equal coordinates are not an extreme point of the \(\ell_1\) ball.

questions.prompt: With fractions \(2/(k + 2)\), the conditional-gradient guarantee of order \(1/k\) bounds
options: the distance \(\lVert x_k - x^\star\rVert\)
the gradient norm alone, with no claim about the gap
the number of vertices the oracle returns
the function gap \(f(x_k) - f^\star\)
questions.explanation: For a smooth convex objective on a compact convex set, the curvature argument gives \(f(x_k) - f^\star \le 2 C_f / (k + 2)\). The left side is the function gap. The distance to a minimizer can stay large while the gap is small, because the method may approach the optimum along a face. The bound does not count oracle vertices. The gradient norm is controlled only indirectly, through that gap.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that drops at first and then flattens.

questions.prompt: On the \(\ell_1\) ball, the gradient is \((3,\ -6,\ 1)\) and the current point is \((1/5,\ -2/5,\ 1/10)\). With fraction \(1/2\), what is the second coordinate of the next point?
questions.explanation: The largest magnitude is \(6\), and that component is negative, so the oracle returns \((0,\ 1,\ 0)\). The update is half the current point plus half the oracle point: the second coordinate is \(\tfrac12 (-2/5) + \tfrac12 (1) = 3/10\). Reporting \(-2/5\) keeps the old coordinate. Reporting \(1\) is the oracle's second coordinate. Reporting \(6\) is the gradient magnitude. The first and third coordinates shrink toward zero and do not affect this component.

questions.prompt: The open-loop fraction \(2/(k + 2)\), with \(k\) counting from \(0\),
options: equals the exact line-search step for every quadratic
is larger than \(1\) for every \(k \ge 0\)
equals \(1\) on the first iteration and decreases toward \(0\)
stays equal to \(1\) at every iteration
questions.explanation: At \(k = 0\) the fraction is \(2/2 = 1\). The denominator grows with \(k\), so later fractions fall toward \(0\) and stay at most \(1\). A constant fraction of \(1\) would jump to a vertex at every iteration. Exact line search minimizes the objective along the segment and depends on the gradient and the curvature, not only on the counter \(k\).
questions.figure_alt: A curve that falls toward the horizontal axis.
